blocks.text: Michaelis, in the Supplemm. vol. III, p. 833, thinks the meaning heap hardly suits this passage. "Where birds are spoken of," he says, "what kind of measure is a heap? For one could make heaps larger or smaller." But what if the writer, as Bochart holds, did not want to define the number precisely? Michaelis adds: "Nor did he remember that, had the quails been gathered into heaps, it would have followed that they grew hot, decayed and stank." But Michaelis did not remember that the quails, as soon as they fell, were gathered by the Israelites and spread out through the camp (v. 32), namely so that they might be dried, just as in the East even today people usually dry fish and meat in the heat of the sun, as Maillet reports, Lettres sur l' Egypte 10, p. 21; 11, p. 110. Michaelis himself would prefer to understand by the word חמרים a certain number of birds joined by a thread passed through them (einen Bund Voegel), from חבר, he joined, which the Arabs would have interchanged with أحمر [aḥmar]. This meaning is unsatisfactory because it lacks support in the usage of the language. Nor can Bochart's suggestion hold, that עשרה, ten, is put for many. For the whole sequence of the words in v. 32 plainly shows that the writer wanted to define precisely the number of quails gathered: there were gathered by him הממעיט, WHO [gathered] LEAST, עשרה חמרים; here, if you put many, there will be no sound sense. And for this very reason, that the writer manifestly wished to give a definite number, I am more inclined to the view of those who think that חמרים is here the name of a measure, namely the cor.
But what prevents us from believing that the quails were gathered in bushels?
But cf. above, note 10, and what Bochart reports below, p. 107, from Gesner, and our note 14.

To these may be added what Aldrovandi, Ornithol. T. II, L. XIII, p. 164, reports in confirmation of this account, from a letter of Franc. Arrivabene of Mantua, chamberlain of Cardinal Paleotti, to Camillo, senator of the city of Bologna, brother of the said Cardinal: I shall gladly tell you what I saw at Nettuno, where we spent three nights. When the most illustrious Cardinal, your brother, set out from here to visit Astura (this is, if I am not mistaken, the name of another town), we had scarcely left the town when we came upon a quail hunt. The nets stretched over four miles, and a very great number of birds was being caught. The fowlers said that they are carried there from Barbary and cross the sea in a single flight, leaving there toward evening and landing here at early morning; that they had sometimes sown in the ground basil seed taken from the birds' crops, and it had germinated successfully, which is certainly proof of a most famous journey. The governor of the place, asked how many had been caught that morning, answered, on the fowlers' reported word, ten thousand and more. Other testimonies from more recent writers have been collected by Oedmann, IV, p. 69, and V, 80.

In this way the most divergent things can be reconciled. But whoever reads will notice that what is read from v. 4 onward happened at another place and time. In the first place (vv. 1, 2, 3) a fire, which arose, it seems, through carelessness, burned part of the camp; superstitious people took this as a punishment for their complaints. Yet it is not reported that anyone perished in that fire. In the other place, however (dealt with from v. 4 onward), a huge multitude of people perished from immoderate eating of quails, which is not obscurely hinted at in these words (v. 20) עד אשר־יצא מאפכם והיה לכם לזרא, and (v. 33) הבשר עודנו בין שניהם. Excessive eating of meat is much more harmful to health in the hot regions of the East than in our lands. This is attested by many who have visited those shores, and Niebuhr too confirms it from his own and his companions' experience in the Praefat. ad Descript. Arab. p. VIII. Moreover, quails, as Aldrovandi asserts, Ornithol. vol. II, p. 171, when eaten rather often [II, 675] and in larger quantity, produce thick, phlegmatic and viscid humors. Others' thoughts on this matter have been presented by Oedmann, Fasc. IV, p. 71 ff., and Fasc. V, p. 79.
